client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately with my thesis deadlines creeping up on me. Balancing that with my part-time job and trying to maintain some social life feels impossible right now. I'm not even sure if talking about it in therapy will help, but I guess I just need to get it off my chest.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load right now, and it’s understandable to feel overwhelmed with all those responsibilities. It’s great that you're reaching out to talk about it, even if you're unsure. What do you think is the most challenging part of managing your thesis and job at the moment?

client: I think the hardest part is just the constant pressure I feel to perform well in both my thesis and my job. It feels like I'm always juggling responsibilities, and whenever I start to make progress in one area, I fall behind in the other. I guess I just feel really overwhelmed and unsure if I can keep up with everything.
therapist: It sounds incredibly stressful to feel that constant pressure to excel in both your thesis and your job, and it's understandable to feel caught in that juggling act. It can be really hard to make progress when it feels like you're always falling behind. Have you considered what specific strategies might help you manage your time and responsibilities more effectively?

client: I really appreciate you understanding how overwhelming it feels to juggle my thesis and job. It’s just that I often feel like I’m not good enough, and making time for strategies seems impossible when I'm already stretched so thin. I worry that even if I tried to implement some new approach, it wouldn't be effective for me, and I'd just end up feeling more frustrated or guilty about not sticking to it.
therapist: I can sense that you’re feeling a lot of pressure and self-doubt about your abilities to manage everything, which can be really discouraging. It’s completely normal to feel hesitant about trying new strategies when you’re already feeling stretched thin. What small step do you think you might be able to take that feels manageable, rather than overwhelming?

client: I guess I do feel a lot of pressure, especially when I think about all the things I have to juggle. It just feels like there’s always something that needs my attention, and I’m worried that even a small step might just add to my anxiety. Sometimes I think about trying something new, but then I wonder if it will really make a difference or if I’ll just end up feeling more overwhelmed.
therapist: It sounds like the pressure is really weighing on you, and it’s understandable to feel hesitant about adding anything new when you're already feeling anxious. It’s tough to think about change when you’re worried it might lead to more overwhelm. What if we explored some small adjustments together that might help lighten that load, without adding too much pressure?

client: I appreciate you understanding how heavy this pressure feels for me. But honestly, the idea of making even small adjustments feels overwhelming right now. I worry that even trying to change anything might just add to my anxiety instead of helping me feel better.
therapist: I can see how the thought of making changes feels daunting when you're already dealing with so much pressure. It's completely valid to be concerned that any new effort might add to your anxiety rather than alleviate it. Let’s take a moment to focus on what’s currently working for you, no matter how small, and see if we can build from there. What’s one thing, however minor, that feels manageable right now?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, I’m not sure there’s anything working for me right now. I feel like I’m just stuck in this cycle of anxiety and guilt, and even thinking about something “manageable” feels overwhelming. It’s hard to believe that anything small could actually make a difference when everything feels so heavy.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling really trapped in this cycle of anxiety and guilt, which must be incredibly frustrating. It’s understandable to doubt that anything could help when everything feels so heavy. Sometimes, just acknowledging these feelings can be a step in itself. What would it feel like to share more about this cycle you’re experiencing?

client: I do feel trapped, and it's hard to see a way out. The anxiety makes me constantly second-guess myself, and then I feel guilty for not handling things better. It’s like I’m stuck in this loop where I can't break free, and sharing it feels overwhelming, like I’m exposing my vulnerabilities.
therapist: It sounds really tough to feel trapped in that loop of anxiety and guilt, and I appreciate you sharing those vulnerable feelings. It’s completely normal to feel exposed when discussing these struggles, but talking about it can also be a way to start finding some clarity. What do you think has been the most challenging belief you hold about yourself in this cycle?

client: I think the most challenging belief I hold about myself is that I'm not good enough, no matter what I do. It’s like this constant pressure that makes me feel I have to prove myself all the time, which only adds to my anxiety and guilt when I don’t meet those expectations. I really struggle with the idea of letting that go, because it feels like if I do, I might lose my drive or sense of purpose.
therapist: It sounds like you’re grappling with some very heavy beliefs about your self-worth, and that pressure to constantly prove yourself can be incredibly draining. It’s understandable to fear that letting go of those expectations might mean losing your drive or sense of purpose, but it’s worth exploring how those beliefs are impacting your well-being. What would it look like for you to redefine what “enough” means for you, without those heavy expectations?

client: I get what you're saying, but honestly, the idea of redefining what "enough" means feels really overwhelming. I’ve built so much of my identity around those expectations, and without them, I worry I’ll just feel lost. It’s hard to imagine what that would even look like, and I fear that if I let go, I might not be motivated to do anything at all.
therapist: I can see how redefining what "enough" means can feel really daunting, especially since those expectations have been such a big part of your identity. It’s completely natural to fear feeling lost without them, and I appreciate you sharing that vulnerability with me. What if we took a step back and explored some small aspects of your identity that aren’t tied to those expectations? What are some things you enjoy or value about yourself outside of your academic and work achievements?

client: I get what you're saying, but honestly, it's hard for me to see myself outside of my achievements. They've always been the way I measure my worth, and without them, I feel like I'm just... nothing. I sometimes think about what I enjoy, but it all feels so insignificant compared to what I've accomplished.
therapist: It sounds like your achievements have become a core part of how you see yourself, and it’s really tough to feel like without them, you’re left with nothing. I can understand why that would make it hard to recognize what you enjoy or value in yourself. What if we took a moment to explore some of those interests or passions, even if they feel small? Sometimes, reconnecting with the things that bring you joy can help shed light on your worth beyond achievements. What’s something that has brought you joy, even if just for a moment?
